# mockito/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)#![warn(missing_docs)]
[2](https://docs.rs#2)#![doc(
[3](https://docs.rs#3)    html_logo_url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lipanski/mockito/master/docs/logo-black-100.png"
[4](https://docs.rs#4))]
[5](https://docs.rs#5)
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//!
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! Mockito is a library for **generating and delivering HTTP mocks** in Rust. You can use it for integration testing
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! or offline work. Mockito runs a local pool of HTTP servers which create, deliver and remove the mocks.
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//!
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! # Features
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//!
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! - Supports HTTP1/2
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! - Runs your tests in parallel
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! - Comes with a wide range of request matchers (Regex, JSON, query parameters etc.)
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! - Checks that a mock was called (spy)
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! - Mocks multiple hosts at the same time
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! - Exposes sync and async interfaces
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! - Prints out a colored diff of the last unmatched request in case of errors
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! - Simple, intuitive API
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! - An awesome logo
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//!
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//! # Getting Started
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//!
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! Add `mockito` to your `Cargo.toml` and start mocking:
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//!
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! ```
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! #[cfg(test)]
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! mod tests {
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//!   #[test]
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//!   fn test_something() {
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//!     // Request a new server from the pool
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//!     let mut server = mockito::Server::new();
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//!
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//!     // Use one of these addresses to configure your client
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//!     let host = server.host_with_port();
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//!     let url = server.url();
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//!
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//!     // Create a mock
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//!     let mock = server.mock("GET", "/hello")
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//!       .with_status(201)
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//!       .with_header("content-type", "text/plain")
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//!       .with_header("x-api-key", "1234")
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//!       .with_body("world")
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!       .create();
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//!
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//!     // Any calls to GET /hello beyond this line will respond with 201, the
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//!     // `content-type: text/plain` header and the body "world".
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//!
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//!     // You can use `Mock::assert` to verify that your mock was called
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//!     // mock.assert();
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//!   }
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! }
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! ```
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! If [`Mock::assert`] fails, a colored diff of the last unmatched request is displayed:
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//!
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! ![colored-diff.png](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lipanski/mockito/master/docs/colored-diff.png)
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//!
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! Use **matchers** to handle requests to the same endpoint in a different way:
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//!
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! ```
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! #[cfg(test)]
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! mod tests {
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//!   #[test]
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//!   fn test_something() {
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//!     let mut server = mockito::Server::new();
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//!
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//!     server.mock("GET", "/greetings")
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//!       .match_header("content-type", "application/json")
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//!       .match_body(mockito::Matcher::PartialJsonString(
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//!           "{\"greeting\": \"hello\"}".to_string(),
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//!       ))
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//!       .with_body("hello json")
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//!       .create();
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//!
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//!     server.mock("GET", "/greetings")
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//!       .match_header("content-type", "application/text")
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//!       .match_body(mockito::Matcher::Regex("greeting=hello".to_string()))
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//!       .with_body("hello text")
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//!       .create();
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//!   }
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! }
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//! ```
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//!
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//! Start **multiple servers** to simulate requests to different hosts:
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//!
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//! ```
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//! #[cfg(test)]
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! mod tests {
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//!   #[test]
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//!   fn test_something() {
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//!     let mut twitter = mockito::Server::new();
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//!     let mut github = mockito::Server::new();
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//!
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//!     // These mocks will be available at `twitter.url()`
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//!     let twitter_mock = twitter.mock("GET", "/api").create();
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//!
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//!     // These mocks will be available at `github.url()`
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//!     let github_mock = github.mock("GET", "/api").create();
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//!   }
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//! }
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! ```
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//!
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! Write **async** tests (make sure to use the `_async` methods!):
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//!
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//! ```
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! #[cfg(test)]
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//! mod tests {
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! # use mockito::Server;
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//!   #[tokio::test]
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//!   async fn test_something() {
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//!     let mut server = Server::new_async().await;
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//!     let m1 = server.mock("GET", "/a").with_body("aaa").create_async().await;
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//!     let m2 = server.mock("GET", "/b").with_body("bbb").create_async().await;
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//!
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//!     let (m1, m2) = futures::join!(m1, m2);
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//!
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//!     // You can use `Mock::assert_async` to verify that your mock was called
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//!     // m1.assert_async().await;
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//!     // m2.assert_async().await;
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//!   }
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//! }
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//! ```
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//!
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//! Start a **stand-alone server** on a dedicated port:
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//!
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//! ```
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//! fn main() {
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//!     let opts = mockito::ServerOpts {
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//!         host: "0.0.0.0",
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//!         port: 1234,
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//!         ..Default::default()
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//!     };
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//!     let mut server = mockito::Server::new_with_opts(opts);
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//!
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//!     let _m = server.mock("GET", "/").with_body("hello world").create();
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//!
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//!     // loop {}
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//! }
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//! ```
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//!
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//! # Lifetime
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//!
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//! A mock is available only throughout the lifetime of the server. Once the server goes
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//! out of scope, all mocks defined on that server are removed:
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//!
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//! ```
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//! let address;
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//!
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//! {
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//!     let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//!     address = s.host_with_port();
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//!
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//!     s.mock("GET", "/").with_body("hi").create();
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//!
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//!     // Requests to `address` will be responded with "hi" til here
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//! }
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//!
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//! // Requests to `address` will fail as of this point
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//! ```
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//!
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//! You can remove individual mocks earlier by calling [`Mock::remove`].
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//!
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//! # Async
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//!
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//! Mockito comes with both a sync and an async interface.
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//!
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//! In order to write async tests, you'll need to use the `*_async` methods:
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//!
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//! - [`Server::new_async`]
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//! - [`Server::new_with_opts_async`]
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//! - [`Mock::create_async`]
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//! - [`Mock::assert_async`]
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//! - [`Mock::matched_async`]
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//! - [`Mock::remove_async`]
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//!
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//! ...otherwise your tests will not compile, and you'll see the following error:
[178](https://docs.rs#178)//!
[179](https://docs.rs#179)//! ```text
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//! Cannot block the current thread from within a runtime.
[181](https://docs.rs#181)//! This happens because a function attempted to block the current thread while the thread is being used to drive asynchronous tasks.
[182](https://docs.rs#182)//! ```
[183](https://docs.rs#183)//!
[184](https://docs.rs#184)//! # Configuring the server
[185](https://docs.rs#185)//!
[186](https://docs.rs#186)//! When calling [`Server::new()`], a mock server with default options is returned from the server
[187](https://docs.rs#187)//! pool. This should suffice for most use cases.
[188](https://docs.rs#188)//!
[189](https://docs.rs#189)//! If you'd like to bypass the server pool or configure the server in a different
[190](https://docs.rs#190)//! way, you can use [`Server::new_with_opts`]. The following **options** are available:
[191](https://docs.rs#191)//!
[192](https://docs.rs#192)//! - `host`: allows setting the host (defaults to `127.0.0.1`)
[193](https://docs.rs#193)//! - `port`: allows setting the port (defaults to a randomly assigned free port)
[194](https://docs.rs#194)//! - `assert_on_drop`: automatically call [`Mock::assert()`] before dropping a mock (defaults to `false`)
[195](https://docs.rs#195)//!
[196](https://docs.rs#196)//! ```
[197](https://docs.rs#197)//! let opts = mockito::ServerOpts { assert_on_drop: true, ..Default::default() };
[198](https://docs.rs#198)//! let server = mockito::Server::new_with_opts(opts);
[199](https://docs.rs#199)//! ```
[200](https://docs.rs#200)//!
[201](https://docs.rs#201)//! # Matchers
[202](https://docs.rs#202)//!
[203](https://docs.rs#203)//! Mockito can match your request by method, path, query, headers or body.
[204](https://docs.rs#204)//!
[205](https://docs.rs#205)//! Various matchers are provided by the [`Matcher`] type: exact (string, binary, JSON), partial (regular expressions,
[206](https://docs.rs#206)//! JSON), any or missing. The following guide will walk you through the most common matchers. Check the
[207](https://docs.rs#207)//! [`Matcher`] documentation for all the rest.
[208](https://docs.rs#208)//!
[209](https://docs.rs#209)//! # Matching by path and query
[210](https://docs.rs#210)//!
[211](https://docs.rs#211)//! By default, the request path and query is compared by its exact value:
[212](https://docs.rs#212)//!
[213](https://docs.rs#213)//! ## Example
[214](https://docs.rs#214)//!
[215](https://docs.rs#215)//! ```
[216](https://docs.rs#216)//! let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
[217](https://docs.rs#217)//!
[218](https://docs.rs#218)//! // Matches only calls to GET /hello
[219](https://docs.rs#219)//! s.mock("GET", "/hello").create();
[220](https://docs.rs#220)//!
[221](https://docs.rs#221)//! // Matches only calls to GET /hello?world=1
[222](https://docs.rs#222)//! s.mock("GET", "/hello?world=1").create();
[223](https://docs.rs#223)//! ```
[224](https://docs.rs#224)//!
[225](https://docs.rs#225)//! You can also match the path partially, by using a regular expression:
[226](https://docs.rs#226)//!
[227](https://docs.rs#227)//! ## Example
[228](https://docs.rs#228)//!
[229](https://docs.rs#229)//! ```
[230](https://docs.rs#230)//! let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
[231](https://docs.rs#231)//!
[232](https://docs.rs#232)//! // Will match calls to GET /hello/1 and GET /hello/2
[233](https://docs.rs#233)//! s.mock("GET",
[234](https://docs.rs#234)//!     mockito::Matcher::Regex(r"^/hello/(1|2)$".to_string())
[235](https://docs.rs#235)//!   ).create();
[236](https://docs.rs#236)//! ```
[237](https://docs.rs#237)//!
[238](https://docs.rs#238)//! Or you can catch all requests, by using the [`Matcher::Any`] variant:
[239](https://docs.rs#239)//!
[240](https://docs.rs#240)//! ## Example
[241](https://docs.rs#241)//!
[242](https://docs.rs#242)//! ```
[243](https://docs.rs#243)//! let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
[244](https://docs.rs#244)//!
[245](https://docs.rs#245)//! // Will match any GET request
[246](https://docs.rs#246)//! s.mock("GET", mockito::Matcher::Any).create();
[247](https://docs.rs#247)//! ```
[248](https://docs.rs#248)//!
[249](https://docs.rs#249)//! # Matching by query
[250](https://docs.rs#250)//!
[251](https://docs.rs#251)//! You can match the query part by using the [`Mock::match_query`] function together with the various matchers,
[252](https://docs.rs#252)//! most notably [`Matcher::UrlEncoded`]:
[253](https://docs.rs#253)//!
[254](https://docs.rs#254)//! ## Example
[255](https://docs.rs#255)//!
[256](https://docs.rs#256)//! ```
[257](https://docs.rs#257)//! let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
[258](https://docs.rs#258)//!
[259](https://docs.rs#259)//! // This will match requests containing the URL-encoded
[260](https://docs.rs#260)//! // query parameter `greeting=good%20day`
[261](https://docs.rs#261)//! s.mock("GET", "/test")
[262](https://docs.rs#262)//!   .match_query(mockito::Matcher::UrlEncoded("greeting".into(), "good day".into()))
[263](https://docs.rs#263)//!   .create();
[264](https://docs.rs#264)//!
[265](https://docs.rs#265)//! // This will match requests containing the URL-encoded
[266](https://docs.rs#266)//! // query parameters `hello=world` and `greeting=good%20day`
[267](https://docs.rs#267)//! s.mock("GET", "/test")
[268](https://docs.rs#268)//!   .match_query(mockito::Matcher::AllOf(vec![
[269](https://docs.rs#269)//!     mockito::Matcher::UrlEncoded("hello".into(), "world".into()),
[270](https://docs.rs#270)//!     mockito::Matcher::UrlEncoded("greeting".into(), "good day".into())
[271](https://docs.rs#271)//!   ]))
[272](https://docs.rs#272)//!   .create();
[273](https://docs.rs#273)//!
[274](https://docs.rs#274)//! // You can achieve similar results with the regex matcher
[275](https://docs.rs#275)//! s.mock("GET", "/test")
[276](https://docs.rs#276)//!   .match_query(mockito::Matcher::Regex("hello=world".into()))
[277](https://docs.rs#277)//!   .create();
[278](https://docs.rs#278)//! ```
[279](https://docs.rs#279)//!
[280](https://docs.rs#280)//! Note that the key/value arguments for [`Matcher::UrlEncoded`] should be left in plain (unencoded) format.
[281](https://docs.rs#281)//!
[282](https://docs.rs#282)//! You can also specify the query as part of the path argument in a [`mock`](Server::mock) call, in which case an exact
[283](https://docs.rs#283)//! match will be performed:
[284](https://docs.rs#284)//!
[285](https://docs.rs#285)//! ## Example
[286](https://docs.rs#286)//!
[287](https://docs.rs#287)//! ```
[288](https://docs.rs#288)//! let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
[289](https://docs.rs#289)//!
[290](https://docs.rs#290)//! // This will perform a full match against the query part
[291](https://docs.rs#291)//! s.mock("GET", "/test?hello=world").create();
[292](https://docs.rs#292)//! ```
[293](https://docs.rs#293)//!
[294](https://docs.rs#294)//! If you'd like to ignore the query entirely, use the [`Matcher::Any`] variant:
[295](https://docs.rs#295)//!
[296](https://docs.rs#296)//! ## Example
[297](https://docs.rs#297)//!
[298](https://docs.rs#298)//! ```
[299](https://docs.rs#299)//! let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
[300](https://docs.rs#300)//!
[301](https://docs.rs#301)//! // This will match requests to GET /test with any query
[302](https://docs.rs#302)//! s.mock("GET", "/test").match_query(mockito::Matcher::Any).create();
[303](https://docs.rs#303)//! ```
[304](https://docs.rs#304)//!
[305](https://docs.rs#305)//! # Matching by header
[306](https://docs.rs#306)//!
[307](https://docs.rs#307)//! By default, headers are compared by their exact value. The header name letter case is ignored though.
[308](https://docs.rs#308)//!
[309](https://docs.rs#309)//! ## Example
[310](https://docs.rs#310)//!
[311](https://docs.rs#311)//! ```
[312](https://docs.rs#312)//! let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
[313](https://docs.rs#313)//!
[314](https://docs.rs#314)//! s.mock("GET", "/hello")
[315](https://docs.rs#315)//!   .match_header("content-type", "application/json")
[316](https://docs.rs#316)//!   .with_body(r#"{"hello": "world"}"#)
[317](https://docs.rs#317)//!   .create();
[318](https://docs.rs#318)//!
[319](https://docs.rs#319)//! s.mock("GET", "/hello")
[320](https://docs.rs#320)//!   .match_header("content-type", "text/plain")
[321](https://docs.rs#321)//!   .with_body("world")
[322](https://docs.rs#322)//!   .create();
[323](https://docs.rs#323)//!
[324](https://docs.rs#324)//! // JSON requests to GET /hello will respond with JSON, while plain requests
[325](https://docs.rs#325)//! // will respond with text.
[326](https://docs.rs#326)//! ```
[327](https://docs.rs#327)//!
[328](https://docs.rs#328)//! You can also match a header value with a *regular expressions*, by using the [`Matcher::Regex`] matcher:
[329](https://docs.rs#329)//!
[330](https://docs.rs#330)//! ## Example
[331](https://docs.rs#331)//!
[332](https://docs.rs#332)//! ```
[333](https://docs.rs#333)//! let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
[334](https://docs.rs#334)//!
[335](https://docs.rs#335)//! s.mock("GET", "/hello")
[336](https://docs.rs#336)//!   .match_header("content-type", mockito::Matcher::Regex(r".*json.*".to_string()))
[337](https://docs.rs#337)//!   .with_body(r#"{"hello": "world"}"#)
[338](https://docs.rs#338)//!   .create();
[339](https://docs.rs#339)//! ```
[340](https://docs.rs#340)//!
[341](https://docs.rs#341)//! Or you can match a header *only by its field name*, by setting the [`Mock::match_header`] value to [`Matcher::Any`].
[342](https://docs.rs#342)//!
[343](https://docs.rs#343)//! ## Example
[344](https://docs.rs#344)//!
[345](https://docs.rs#345)//! ```
[346](https://docs.rs#346)//! let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
[347](https://docs.rs#347)//!
[348](https://docs.rs#348)//! s.mock("GET", "/hello")
[349](https://docs.rs#349)//!  .match_header("content-type", mockito::Matcher::Any)
[350](https://docs.rs#350)//!  .with_body("something")
[351](https://docs.rs#351)//!  .create();
[352](https://docs.rs#352)//!
[353](https://docs.rs#353)//! // Requests containing any content-type header value will be mocked.
[354](https://docs.rs#354)//! // Requests not containing this header will return `501 Not Implemented`.
[355](https://docs.rs#355)//! ```
[356](https://docs.rs#356)//!
[357](https://docs.rs#357)//! You can mock requests that should be *missing a particular header field*, by setting the [`Mock::match_header`]
[358](https://docs.rs#358)//! value to [`Matcher::Missing`].
[359](https://docs.rs#359)//!
[360](https://docs.rs#360)//! ## Example
[361](https://docs.rs#361)//!
[362](https://docs.rs#362)//! ```
[363](https://docs.rs#363)//! let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
[364](https://docs.rs#364)//!
[365](https://docs.rs#365)//! s.mock("GET", "/hello")
[366](https://docs.rs#366)//!   .match_header("authorization", mockito::Matcher::Missing)
[367](https://docs.rs#367)//!   .with_body("no authorization header")
[368](https://docs.rs#368)//!   .create();
[369](https://docs.rs#369)//!
[370](https://docs.rs#370)//! // Requests without the authorization header will be matched.
[371](https://docs.rs#371)//! // Requests containing the authorization header will return `501 Mock Not Found`.
[372](https://docs.rs#372)//! ```
[373](https://docs.rs#373)//!
[374](https://docs.rs#374)//! # Matching by body
[375](https://docs.rs#375)//!
[376](https://docs.rs#376)//! You can match a request by its body by using the [`Mock::match_body`] method.
[377](https://docs.rs#377)//! By default, the request body is ignored, similar to passing the [`Matcher::Any`] argument to the [`Mock::match_body`] method.
[378](https://docs.rs#378)//!
[379](https://docs.rs#379)//! You can match a body by an exact value:
[380](https://docs.rs#380)//!
[381](https://docs.rs#381)//! ## Example
[382](https://docs.rs#382)//!
[383](https://docs.rs#383)//! ```
[384](https://docs.rs#384)//! let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
[385](https://docs.rs#385)//!
[386](https://docs.rs#386)//! // Will match requests to POST / whenever the request body is "hello"
[387](https://docs.rs#387)//! s.mock("POST", "/").match_body("hello").create();
[388](https://docs.rs#388)//! ```
[389](https://docs.rs#389)//!
[390](https://docs.rs#390)//! Or you can match the body by using a regular expression:
[391](https://docs.rs#391)//!
[392](https://docs.rs#392)//! ## Example
[393](https://docs.rs#393)//!
[394](https://docs.rs#394)//! ```
[395](https://docs.rs#395)//! let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
[396](https://docs.rs#396)//!
[397](https://docs.rs#397)//! // Will match requests to POST / whenever the request body *contains* the word "hello" (e.g. "hello world")
[398](https://docs.rs#398)//! s.mock("POST", "/").match_body(
[399](https://docs.rs#399)//!     mockito::Matcher::Regex("hello".to_string())
[400](https://docs.rs#400)//!   ).create();
[401](https://docs.rs#401)//! ```
[402](https://docs.rs#402)//!
[403](https://docs.rs#403)//! Or you can match the body using a JSON object:
[404](https://docs.rs#404)//!
[405](https://docs.rs#405)//! ## Example
[406](https://docs.rs#406)//!
[407](https://docs.rs#407)//! ```
[408](https://docs.rs#408)//! # extern crate mockito;
[409](https://docs.rs#409)//! #[macro_use]
[410](https://docs.rs#410)//! extern crate serde_json;
[411](https://docs.rs#411)//!
[412](https://docs.rs#412)//! # fn main() {
[413](https://docs.rs#413)//! let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
[414](https://docs.rs#414)//! // Will match requests to POST / whenever the request body matches the json object
[415](https://docs.rs#415)//! s.mock("POST", "/").match_body(mockito::Matcher::Json(json!({"hello": "world"}))).create();
[416](https://docs.rs#416)//! # }
[417](https://docs.rs#417)//! ```
[418](https://docs.rs#418)//!
[419](https://docs.rs#419)//! If `serde_json::json!` is not exposed, you can use [`Matcher::JsonString`] the same way,
[420](https://docs.rs#420)//! but by passing a `String` to the matcher:
[421](https://docs.rs#421)//!
[422](https://docs.rs#422)//! ```
[423](https://docs.rs#423)//! let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
[424](https://docs.rs#424)//!
[425](https://docs.rs#425)//! // Will match requests to POST / whenever the request body matches the json object
[426](https://docs.rs#426)//! s.mock("POST", "/")
[427](https://docs.rs#427)//!     .match_body(
[428](https://docs.rs#428)//!        mockito::Matcher::JsonString(r#"{"hello": "world"}"#.to_string())
[429](https://docs.rs#429)//!     )
[430](https://docs.rs#430)//!     .create();
[431](https://docs.rs#431)//! ```
[432](https://docs.rs#432)//!
[433](https://docs.rs#433)//! # The `AnyOf` matcher
[434](https://docs.rs#434)//!
[435](https://docs.rs#435)//! The [`Matcher::AnyOf`] construct takes a vector of matchers as arguments and will be enabled
[436](https://docs.rs#436)//! if at least one of the provided matchers matches the request.
[437](https://docs.rs#437)//!
[438](https://docs.rs#438)//! ## Example
[439](https://docs.rs#439)//!
[440](https://docs.rs#440)//! ```
[441](https://docs.rs#441)//! let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
[442](https://docs.rs#442)//!
[443](https://docs.rs#443)//! // Will match requests to POST / whenever the request body is either `hello=world` or `{"hello":"world"}`
[444](https://docs.rs#444)//! s.mock("POST", "/")
[445](https://docs.rs#445)//!     .match_body(
[446](https://docs.rs#446)//!         mockito::Matcher::AnyOf(vec![
[447](https://docs.rs#447)//!             mockito::Matcher::Exact("hello=world".to_string()),
[448](https://docs.rs#448)//!             mockito::Matcher::JsonString(r#"{"hello": "world"}"#.to_string()),
[449](https://docs.rs#449)//!         ])
[450](https://docs.rs#450)//!      )
[451](https://docs.rs#451)//!     .create();
[452](https://docs.rs#452)//! ```
[453](https://docs.rs#453)//!
[454](https://docs.rs#454)//! # The `AllOf` matcher
[455](https://docs.rs#455)//!
[456](https://docs.rs#456)//! The [`Matcher::AllOf`] construct takes a vector of matchers as arguments and will be enabled
[457](https://docs.rs#457)//! if all the provided matchers match the request.
[458](https://docs.rs#458)//!
[459](https://docs.rs#459)//! ## Example
[460](https://docs.rs#460)//!
[461](https://docs.rs#461)//! ```
[462](https://docs.rs#462)//! let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
[463](https://docs.rs#463)//!
[464](https://docs.rs#464)//! // Will match requests to POST / whenever the request body contains both `hello` and `world`
[465](https://docs.rs#465)//! s.mock("POST", "/")
[466](https://docs.rs#466)//!     .match_body(
[467](https://docs.rs#467)//!         mockito::Matcher::AllOf(vec![
[468](https://docs.rs#468)//!             mockito::Matcher::Regex("hello".to_string()),
[469](https://docs.rs#469)//!             mockito::Matcher::Regex("world".to_string()),
[470](https://docs.rs#470)//!         ])
[471](https://docs.rs#471)//!      )
[472](https://docs.rs#472)//!     .create();
[473](https://docs.rs#473)//! ```
[474](https://docs.rs#474)//!
[475](https://docs.rs#475)//! # Custom matchers
[476](https://docs.rs#476)//!
[477](https://docs.rs#477)//! If you need a more custom matcher, you can use the [`Mock::match_request`] function, which
[478](https://docs.rs#478)//! takes a closure and exposes the [`Request`] object as an argument. The closure should return
[479](https://docs.rs#479)//! a boolean value.
[480](https://docs.rs#480)//!
[481](https://docs.rs#481)//! ## Example
[482](https://docs.rs#482)//!
[483](https://docs.rs#483)//! ```
[484](https://docs.rs#484)//! use mockito::Matcher;
[485](https://docs.rs#485)//!
[486](https://docs.rs#486)//! let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
[487](https://docs.rs#487)//!
[488](https://docs.rs#488)//! // This will match requests that have the x-test header set
[489](https://docs.rs#489)//! // and contain the word "hello" inside the body
[490](https://docs.rs#490)//! s.mock("GET", "/")
[491](https://docs.rs#491)//!     .match_request(|request| {
[492](https://docs.rs#492)//!         request.has_header("x-test") &&
[493](https://docs.rs#493)//!             request.utf8_lossy_body().unwrap().contains("hello")
[494](https://docs.rs#494)//!     })
[495](https://docs.rs#495)//!     .create();
[496](https://docs.rs#496)//! ```
[497](https://docs.rs#497)//!
[498](https://docs.rs#498)//! # Asserts
[499](https://docs.rs#499)//!
[500](https://docs.rs#500)//! You can use the [`Mock::assert`] method to **assert that a mock was called**. In other words,
[501](https://docs.rs#501)//! `Mock#assert` can validate that your code performed the expected HTTP request.
[502](https://docs.rs#502)//!
[503](https://docs.rs#503)//! By default, the method expects only **one** request to your mock.
[504](https://docs.rs#504)//!
[505](https://docs.rs#505)//! ## Example
[506](https://docs.rs#506)//!
[507](https://docs.rs#507)//! ```no_run
[508](https://docs.rs#508)//! use std::net::TcpStream;
[509](https://docs.rs#509)//! use std::io::{Read, Write};
[510](https://docs.rs#510)//!
[511](https://docs.rs#511)//! let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
[512](https://docs.rs#512)//! let mock = s.mock("GET", "/hello").create();
[513](https://docs.rs#513)//!
[514](https://docs.rs#514)//! {
[515](https://docs.rs#515)//!     // Place a request
[516](https://docs.rs#516)//!     let mut stream = TcpStream::connect(s.host_with_port()).unwrap();
[517](https://docs.rs#517)//!     stream.write_all("GET /hello HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n".as_bytes()).unwrap();
[518](https://docs.rs#518)//!     let mut response = String::new();
[519](https://docs.rs#519)//!     stream.read_to_string(&mut response).unwrap();
[520](https://docs.rs#520)//!     stream.flush().unwrap();
[521](https://docs.rs#521)//! }
[522](https://docs.rs#522)//!
[523](https://docs.rs#523)//! mock.assert();
[524](https://docs.rs#524)//! ```
[525](https://docs.rs#525)//!
[526](https://docs.rs#526)//! When several mocks can match a request, Mockito applies the first one that still expects requests.
[527](https://docs.rs#527)//! You can use this behaviour to provide **different responses for subsequent requests to the same endpoint**.
[528](https://docs.rs#528)//!
[529](https://docs.rs#529)//! ## Example
[530](https://docs.rs#530)//!
[531](https://docs.rs#531)//! ```
[532](https://docs.rs#532)//! use std::net::TcpStream;
[533](https://docs.rs#533)//! use std::io::{Read, Write};
[534](https://docs.rs#534)//!
[535](https://docs.rs#535)//! let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
[536](https://docs.rs#536)//! let english_hello_mock = s.mock("GET", "/hello").with_body("good bye").create();
[537](https://docs.rs#537)//! let french_hello_mock = s.mock("GET", "/hello").with_body("au revoir").create();
[538](https://docs.rs#538)//!
[539](https://docs.rs#539)//! {
[540](https://docs.rs#540)//!     // Place a request to GET /hello
[541](https://docs.rs#541)//!     let mut stream = TcpStream::connect(s.host_with_port()).unwrap();
[542](https://docs.rs#542)//!     stream.write_all("GET /hello HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n".as_bytes()).unwrap();
[543](https://docs.rs#543)//!     let mut response = String::new();
[544](https://docs.rs#544)//!     stream.read_to_string(&mut response).unwrap();
[545](https://docs.rs#545)//!     stream.flush().unwrap();
[546](https://docs.rs#546)//! }
[547](https://docs.rs#547)//!
[548](https://docs.rs#548)//! english_hello_mock.assert();
[549](https://docs.rs#549)//!
[550](https://docs.rs#550)//! {
[551](https://docs.rs#551)//!     // Place another request to GET /hello
[552](https://docs.rs#552)//!     let mut stream = TcpStream::connect(s.host_with_port()).unwrap();
[553](https://docs.rs#553)//!     stream.write_all("GET /hello HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n".as_bytes()).unwrap();
[554](https://docs.rs#554)//!     let mut response = String::new();
[555](https://docs.rs#555)//!     stream.read_to_string(&mut response).unwrap();
[556](https://docs.rs#556)//!     stream.flush().unwrap();
[557](https://docs.rs#557)//! }
[558](https://docs.rs#558)//!
[559](https://docs.rs#559)//! french_hello_mock.assert();
[560](https://docs.rs#560)//! ```
[561](https://docs.rs#561)//!
[562](https://docs.rs#562)//! If you're expecting more than 1 request, you can use the [`Mock::expect`] method to specify the exact amount of requests:
[563](https://docs.rs#563)//!
[564](https://docs.rs#564)//! ## Example
[565](https://docs.rs#565)//!
[566](https://docs.rs#566)//! ```no_run
[567](https://docs.rs#567)//! use std::net::TcpStream;
[568](https://docs.rs#568)//! use std::io::{Read, Write};
[569](https://docs.rs#569)//!
[570](https://docs.rs#570)//! let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
[571](https://docs.rs#571)//!
[572](https://docs.rs#572)//! let mock = s.mock("GET", "/hello").expect(3).create();
[573](https://docs.rs#573)//!
[574](https://docs.rs#574)//! for _ in 0..3 {
[575](https://docs.rs#575)//!     // Place a request
[576](https://docs.rs#576)//!     let mut stream = TcpStream::connect(s.host_with_port()).unwrap();
[577](https://docs.rs#577)//!     stream.write_all("GET /hello HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n".as_bytes()).unwrap();
[578](https://docs.rs#578)//!     let mut response = String::new();
[579](https://docs.rs#579)//!     stream.read_to_string(&mut response).unwrap();
[580](https://docs.rs#580)//!     stream.flush().unwrap();
[581](https://docs.rs#581)//! }
[582](https://docs.rs#582)//!
[583](https://docs.rs#583)//! mock.assert();
[584](https://docs.rs#584)//! ```
[585](https://docs.rs#585)//!
[586](https://docs.rs#586)//! You can also work with ranges, by using the [`Mock::expect_at_least`] and [`Mock::expect_at_most`] methods:
[587](https://docs.rs#587)//!
[588](https://docs.rs#588)//! ## Example
[589](https://docs.rs#589)//!
[590](https://docs.rs#590)//! ```no_run
[591](https://docs.rs#591)//! use std::net::TcpStream;
[592](https://docs.rs#592)//! use std::io::{Read, Write};
[593](https://docs.rs#593)//!
[594](https://docs.rs#594)//! let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
[595](https://docs.rs#595)//!
[596](https://docs.rs#596)//! let mock = s.mock("GET", "/hello").expect_at_least(2).expect_at_most(4).create();
[597](https://docs.rs#597)//!
[598](https://docs.rs#598)//! for _ in 0..3 {
[599](https://docs.rs#599)//!     // Place a request
[600](https://docs.rs#600)//!     let mut stream = TcpStream::connect(s.host_with_port()).unwrap();
[601](https://docs.rs#601)//!     stream.write_all("GET /hello HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n".as_bytes()).unwrap();
[602](https://docs.rs#602)//!     let mut response = String::new();
[603](https://docs.rs#603)//!     stream.read_to_string(&mut response).unwrap();
[604](https://docs.rs#604)//!     stream.flush().unwrap();
[605](https://docs.rs#605)//! }
[606](https://docs.rs#606)//!
[607](https://docs.rs#607)//! mock.assert();
[608](https://docs.rs#608)//! ```
[609](https://docs.rs#609)//!
[610](https://docs.rs#610)//! The errors produced by the [`Mock::assert`] method contain information about the tested mock, but also about the
[611](https://docs.rs#611)//! **last unmatched request**, which can be very useful to track down an error in your implementation or
[612](https://docs.rs#612)//! a missing or incomplete mock. A colored diff is also displayed:
[613](https://docs.rs#613)//!
[614](https://docs.rs#614)//! ![colored-diff.png](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lipanski/mockito/master/docs/colored-diff.png)
[615](https://docs.rs#615)//!
[616](https://docs.rs#616)//! Color output is enabled by default, but can be toggled with the `color` feature flag.
[617](https://docs.rs#617)//!
[618](https://docs.rs#618)//! Here's an example of how a [`Mock::assert`] error looks like:
[619](https://docs.rs#619)//!
[620](https://docs.rs#620)//! ```text
[621](https://docs.rs#621)//! > Expected 1 request(s) to:
[622](https://docs.rs#622)//!
[623](https://docs.rs#623)//! POST /users?number=one
[624](https://docs.rs#624)//! bob
[625](https://docs.rs#625)//!
[626](https://docs.rs#626)//! ...but received 0
[627](https://docs.rs#627)//!
[628](https://docs.rs#628)//! > The last unmatched request was:
[629](https://docs.rs#629)//!
[630](https://docs.rs#630)//! POST /users?number=two
[631](https://docs.rs#631)//! content-length: 5
[632](https://docs.rs#632)//! alice
[633](https://docs.rs#633)//!
[634](https://docs.rs#634)//! > Difference:
[635](https://docs.rs#635)//!
[636](https://docs.rs#636)//! # A colored diff
[637](https://docs.rs#637)//!
[638](https://docs.rs#638)//! ```
[639](https://docs.rs#639)//!
[640](https://docs.rs#640)//! You can also use the [`Mock::matched`] method to return a boolean for whether the mock was called the
[641](https://docs.rs#641)//! correct number of times without panicking
[642](https://docs.rs#642)//!
[643](https://docs.rs#643)//! ## Example
[644](https://docs.rs#644)//!
[645](https://docs.rs#645)//! ```
[646](https://docs.rs#646)//! use std::net::TcpStream;
[647](https://docs.rs#647)//! use std::io::{Read, Write};
[648](https://docs.rs#648)//!
[649](https://docs.rs#649)//! let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
[650](https://docs.rs#650)//!
[651](https://docs.rs#651)//! let mock = s.mock("GET", "/").create();
[652](https://docs.rs#652)//!
[653](https://docs.rs#653)//! {
[654](https://docs.rs#654)//!     let mut stream = TcpStream::connect(s.host_with_port()).unwrap();
[655](https://docs.rs#655)//!     stream.write_all("GET / HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n".as_bytes()).unwrap();
[656](https://docs.rs#656)//!     let mut response = String::new();
[657](https://docs.rs#657)//!     stream.read_to_string(&mut response).unwrap();
[658](https://docs.rs#658)//!     stream.flush().unwrap();
[659](https://docs.rs#659)//! }
[660](https://docs.rs#660)//!
[661](https://docs.rs#661)//! assert!(mock.matched());
[662](https://docs.rs#662)//!
[663](https://docs.rs#663)//! {
[664](https://docs.rs#664)//!     let mut stream = TcpStream::connect(s.host_with_port()).unwrap();
[665](https://docs.rs#665)//!     stream.write_all("GET / HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n".as_bytes()).unwrap();
[666](https://docs.rs#666)//!     let mut response = String::new();
[667](https://docs.rs#667)//!     stream.read_to_string(&mut response).unwrap();
[668](https://docs.rs#668)//!     stream.flush().unwrap();
[669](https://docs.rs#669)//! }
[670](https://docs.rs#670)//! assert!(!mock.matched());
[671](https://docs.rs#671)//! ```
[672](https://docs.rs#672)//!
[673](https://docs.rs#673)//! # Non-matching calls
[674](https://docs.rs#674)//!
[675](https://docs.rs#675)//! Any calls to the Mockito server that are not matched will return *501 Not Implemented*.
[676](https://docs.rs#676)//!
[677](https://docs.rs#677)//! Note that **mocks are matched in the order they are defined**.
[678](https://docs.rs#678)//!
[679](https://docs.rs#679)//! # Cleaning up
[680](https://docs.rs#680)//!
[681](https://docs.rs#681)//! As mentioned earlier, mocks are cleaned up whenever the server goes out of scope. If you
[682](https://docs.rs#682)//! need to remove them earlier, you can call [`Server::reset`] to remove all mocks registered
[683](https://docs.rs#683)//! so far:
[684](https://docs.rs#684)//!
[685](https://docs.rs#685)//! ```
[686](https://docs.rs#686)//! let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
[687](https://docs.rs#687)//!
[688](https://docs.rs#688)//! s.mock("GET", "/1").create();
[689](https://docs.rs#689)//! s.mock("GET", "/2").create();
[690](https://docs.rs#690)//! s.mock("GET", "/3").create();
[691](https://docs.rs#691)//!
[692](https://docs.rs#692)//! s.reset();
[693](https://docs.rs#693)//!
[694](https://docs.rs#694)//! // Nothing is mocked at this point
[695](https://docs.rs#695)//! ```
[696](https://docs.rs#696)//!
[697](https://docs.rs#697)//! ...or you can call [`Mock::remove`] to remove a single mock:
[698](https://docs.rs#698)//!
[699](https://docs.rs#699)//! ```
[700](https://docs.rs#700)//! let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
[701](https://docs.rs#701)//!
[702](https://docs.rs#702)//! let m1 = s.mock("GET", "/1").create();
[703](https://docs.rs#703)//! let m2 = s.mock("GET", "/2").create();
[704](https://docs.rs#704)//!
[705](https://docs.rs#705)//! m1.remove();
[706](https://docs.rs#706)//!
[707](https://docs.rs#707)//! // Only m2 is available at this point
[708](https://docs.rs#708)//! ```
[709](https://docs.rs#709)//!
[710](https://docs.rs#710)//! # Debug
[711](https://docs.rs#711)//!
[712](https://docs.rs#712)//! Mockito uses the `env_logger` crate under the hood to provide useful debugging information.
[713](https://docs.rs#713)//!
[714](https://docs.rs#714)//! If you'd like to activate the debug output, introduce the [env_logger](https://crates.rs/crates/env_logger) crate
[715](https://docs.rs#715)//! to your project and initialize it before each test that needs debugging:
[716](https://docs.rs#716)//!
[717](https://docs.rs#717)//! ```
[718](https://docs.rs#718)//! #[test]
[719](https://docs.rs#719)//! fn example_test() {
[720](https://docs.rs#720)//!     let _ = env_logger::try_init();
[721](https://docs.rs#721)//!     // ...
[722](https://docs.rs#722)//! }
[723](https://docs.rs#723)//! ```
[724](https://docs.rs#724)//!
[725](https://docs.rs#725)//! Run your tests with:
[726](https://docs.rs#726)//!

# Mock in mockito - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mockito/1.7.2/mockito/struct.Mock.html

`pub struct Mock { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Stores information about a mocked request. Should be initialized via `Server::mock()`.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/mockito/mock.rs.html#213-226)#### pub fn [match_query](https://docs.rs#method.match_query)<M: [Into](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.Into.html)<[Matcher](https://docs.rs/enum.Matcher.html)>>(self, query: M) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/mockito/mock.rs.html#213-226)

#### pub fn [match_query](https://docs.rs#method.match_query)<M: [Into](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.Into.html)<[Matcher](https://docs.rs/enum.Matcher.html)>>(self, query: M) -> Self

Allows matching against the query part when responding with a mock.

Note that you can also specify the query as part of the path argument
in a `mock` call, in which case an exact match will be performed.
Any future calls of `Mock#match_query` will override the query matcher.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use mockito::Matcher;
let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
// This will match requests containing the URL-encoded
// query parameter `greeting=good%20day`
s.mock("GET", "/test")
  .match_query(Matcher::UrlEncoded("greeting".into(), "good day".into()))
  .create();
// This will match requests containing the URL-encoded
// query parameters `hello=world` and `greeting=good%20day`
s.mock("GET", "/test")
  .match_query(Matcher::AllOf(vec![
    Matcher::UrlEncoded("hello".into(), "world".into()),
    Matcher::UrlEncoded("greeting".into(), "good day".into())
  ]))
  .create();
// You can achieve similar results with the regex matcher
s.mock("GET", "/test")
  .match_query(Matcher::Regex("hello=world".into()))
  .create();
```

Allows matching a particular request header when responding with a mock.

When matching a request, the field letter case is ignored.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

```
let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
s.mock("GET", "/").match_header("content-type", "application/json");

Like most other `Mock` methods, it allows chanining:

s.mock("GET", "/")

#### pub fn [match_body](https://docs.rs#method.match_body)<M: [Into](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.Into.html)<[Matcher](https://docs.rs/enum.Matcher.html)>>(self, body: M) -> Self

Allows matching a particular request body when responding with a mock.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-3)Example

```
let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
s.mock("POST", "/").match_body(r#"{"hello": "world"}"#).with_body("json").create();
s.mock("POST", "/").match_body("hello=world").with_body("form").create();
// Requests passing `{"hello": "world"}` inside the body will be responded with "json".
// Requests passing `hello=world` inside the body will be responded with "form".
// Create a temporary file
use std::env;
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::Write;
use std::path::Path;
use rand;
use rand::Rng;
let random_bytes: Vec<u8> = (0..1024).map(|_| rand::random::<u8>()).collect();
let mut tmp_file = env::temp_dir();
tmp_file.push("test_file.txt");
let mut f_write = File::create(tmp_file.clone()).unwrap();
f_write.write_all(random_bytes.as_slice()).unwrap();
let mut f_read = File::open(tmp_file.clone()).unwrap();
// the following are equivalent ways of defining a mock matching
// a binary payload
s.mock("POST", "/").match_body(tmp_file.as_path()).create();
s.mock("POST", "/").match_body(random_bytes).create();
s.mock("POST", "/").match_body(&mut f_read).create();
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/mockito/mock.rs.html#327-334)

#### pub fn [match_request](https://docs.rs#method.match_request)<F>(self, request_matcher: F) -> Self

Allows matching the entire request based on a closure that takes
the [ Request](https://docs.rs/struct.Request.html) object as an argument and returns a boolean value.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-4)Example

```
use mockito::Matcher;
let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
// This will match requests that have the x-test header set
// and contain the word "hello" inside the body
s.mock("GET", "/")
    .match_request(|request| {
        request.has_header("x-test") &&
            request.utf8_lossy_body().unwrap().contains("hello")
    })
    .create();
```

Sets the status code of the mock response dynamically while exposing the request object.

You can use this method to provide custom status code for every incoming request.

The function must be thread-safe. If it’s a closure, it can’t be borrowing its context.
Use `move` closures and `Arc` to share any data.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-6)Example

```
let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
let _m = s.mock("GET", mockito::Matcher::Any).with_status_code_from_request(|request| {
    if request.path() == "/bob" {
        500
    } else if request.path() == "/alice" {
        400
    } else {
        404
    }
});
```

Sets the body of the mock response dynamically. The response will use chunked transfer encoding.

The callback function will be called only once. You can sleep in between calls to the writer to simulate delays between the chunks. The callback function can also return an error after any number of writes in order to abort the response.

The function must be thread-safe. If it’s a closure, it can’t be borrowing its context.
Use `move` closures and `Arc` to share any data.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-10)Example

```
let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
s.mock("GET", "/").with_chunked_body(|w| w.write_all(b"hello world"));
```

# Server in mockito - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mockito/1.7.2/mockito/struct.Server.html

`pub struct Server { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

One instance of the mock server.

Mockito uses a server pool to manage running servers. Once the pool reaches capacity, new requests will have to wait for a free server. The size of the server pool is set to 50.

Most of the times, you should initialize new servers with `Server::new`, which fetches
the next available instance from the pool:

`let mut server = mockito::Server::new();`If you’d like to bypass the server pool or configure the server in a different way
(by setting a custom host and port or enabling auto-asserts), you can use `Server::new_with_opts`:

```
let opts = mockito::ServerOpts { port: 0, ..Default::default() };
let server_with_port = mockito::Server::new_with_opts(opts);
let opts = mockito::ServerOpts { host: "0.0.0.0", ..Default::default() };
let server_with_host = mockito::Server::new_with_opts(opts);
let opts = mockito::ServerOpts { assert_on_drop: true, ..Default::default() };
let server_with_auto_assert = mockito::Server::new_with_opts(opts);
```
## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

# Matcher in mockito - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mockito/1.7.2/mockito/enum.Matcher.html

```
pub enum Matcher {
    Exact(
```
[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)),
    Binary(BinaryBody),
    Regex([String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)),
    Json([Value](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1.0.108/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_json/value/enum.Value.html)),
    JsonString([String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)),
    PartialJson([Value](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1.0.108/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_json/value/enum.Value.html)),
    PartialJsonString([String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)),
    UrlEncoded([String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html), [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)),
    AnyOf([Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[Matcher](https://docs.rs/enum.Matcher.html)>),
    AllOf([Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[Matcher](https://docs.rs/enum.Matcher.html)>),
    Any,
    Missing,
}## Expand description

Allows matching the request path, headers or body in multiple ways: by the exact value, by any value (as long as it is present), by regular expression or by checking that a particular header is missing.

These matchers can be used within the `Server::mock`, `Mock::match_header` or `Mock::match_body` calls.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Exact)

### Exact([String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html))

Matches the exact path or header value. There’s also an implementation of `From<&str>`
to keep things simple and backwards compatible.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Binary)

### Binary(BinaryBody)

Matches the body content as a binary file

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Regex)

### Regex([String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html))

Matches a path or header value by a regular expression.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Json)

### Json([Value](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1.0.108/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_json/value/enum.Value.html))

Matches a specified JSON body from a `serde_json::Value`

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.JsonString)

### JsonString([String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html))

Matches a specified JSON body from a `String`

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.PartialJson)

### PartialJson([Value](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1.0.108/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_json/value/enum.Value.html))

Matches a partial JSON body from a `serde_json::Value`

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.PartialJsonString)

### PartialJsonString([String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html))

Matches a specified partial JSON body from a `String`

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.UrlEncoded)

Matches a URL-encoded key/value pair, where both key and value should be specified in plain (unencoded) format

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.AnyOf)

At least one matcher must match

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.AllOf)

All matchers must match

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Any)

### Any

Matches any path or any header value.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Missing)

### Missing

Checks that a header is not present in the request.

# ServerGuard in mockito - Rust

A handle around a pooled `Server` object which dereferences to `Server`.

Initializes a mock with the given HTTP `method` and `path`.

The mock is enabled on the server only after calling the `Mock::create` method.

let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
let _m1 = s.mock("GET", "/");
let _m2 = s.mock("POST", "/users");

# mockito - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mockito/latest/mockito/

## Expand description

Mockito is a library for **generating and delivering HTTP mocks** in Rust. You can use it for integration testing
or offline work. Mockito runs a local pool of HTTP servers which create, deliver and remove the mocks.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- Supports HTTP1/2
- Runs your tests in parallel
- Comes with a wide range of request matchers (Regex, JSON, query parameters etc.)
- Checks that a mock was called (spy)
- Mocks multiple hosts at the same time
- Exposes sync and async interfaces
- Prints out a colored diff of the last unmatched request in case of errors
- Simple, intuitive API
- An awesome logo

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting Started

Add `mockito` to your `Cargo.toml` and start mocking:

```
#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
  #[test]
  fn test_something() {
    // Request a new server from the pool
    let mut server = mockito::Server::new();
    // Use one of these addresses to configure your client
    let host = server.host_with_port();
    let url = server.url();
    // Create a mock
    let mock = server.mock("GET", "/hello")
      .with_status(201)
      .with_header("content-type", "text/plain")
      .with_header("x-api-key", "1234")
      .with_body("world")
      .create();
    // Any calls to GET /hello beyond this line will respond with 201, the
    // `content-type: text/plain` header and the body "world".
    // You can use `Mock::assert` to verify that your mock was called
    // mock.assert();
  }
}
```
If [ Mock::assert](https://docs.rs/struct.Mock.html#method.assert) fails, a colored diff of the last unmatched request is displayed:

Use **matchers** to handle requests to the same endpoint in a different way:

```
#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
  #[test]
  fn test_something() {
    let mut server = mockito::Server::new();
    server.mock("GET", "/greetings")
      .match_header("content-type", "application/json")
      .match_body(mockito::Matcher::PartialJsonString(
          "{\"greeting\": \"hello\"}".to_string(),
      ))
      .with_body("hello json")
      .create();
    server.mock("GET", "/greetings")
      .match_header("content-type", "application/text")
      .match_body(mockito::Matcher::Regex("greeting=hello".to_string()))
      .with_body("hello text")
      .create();
  }
}
```
Start **multiple servers** to simulate requests to different hosts:

```
#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
  #[test]
  fn test_something() {
    let mut twitter = mockito::Server::new();
    let mut github = mockito::Server::new();
    // These mocks will be available at `twitter.url()`
    let twitter_mock = twitter.mock("GET", "/api").create();
    // These mocks will be available at `github.url()`
    let github_mock = github.mock("GET", "/api").create();
  }
}
```
Write **async** tests (make sure to use the `_async` methods!):

```
#[cfg(test)]
mod tests {
  #[tokio::test]
  async fn test_something() {
    let mut server = Server::new_async().await;
    let m1 = server.mock("GET", "/a").with_body("aaa").create_async().await;
    let m2 = server.mock("GET", "/b").with_body("bbb").create_async().await;
    let (m1, m2) = futures::join!(m1, m2);
    // You can use `Mock::assert_async` to verify that your mock was called
    // m1.assert_async().await;
    // m2.assert_async().await;
  }
}
```
Start a **stand-alone server** on a dedicated port:

```
fn main() {
    let opts = mockito::ServerOpts {
        host: "0.0.0.0",
        port: 1234,
        ..Default::default()
    };
    let mut server = mockito::Server::new_with_opts(opts);
    let _m = server.mock("GET", "/").with_body("hello world").create();
    // loop {}
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#lifetime)Lifetime

A mock is available only throughout the lifetime of the server. Once the server goes out of scope, all mocks defined on that server are removed:

```
let address;
{
    let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
    address = s.host_with_port();
    s.mock("GET", "/").with_body("hi").create();
    // Requests to `address` will be responded with "hi" til here
}
// Requests to `address` will fail as of this point
```
You can remove individual mocks earlier by calling [ Mock::remove](https://docs.rs/struct.Mock.html#method.remove).

[§](https://docs.rs#async)Async

Mockito comes with both a sync and an async interface.

In order to write async tests, you’ll need to use the `*_async` methods:

- `Server::new_async`
- `Server::new_with_opts_async`
- `Mock::create_async`
- `Mock::assert_async`
- `Mock::matched_async`
- `Mock::remove_async`

…otherwise your tests will not compile, and you’ll see the following error:

```
Cannot block the current thread from within a runtime.
This happens because a function attempted to block the current thread while the thread is being used to drive asynchronous tasks.
```
[§](https://docs.rs#configuring-the-server)Configuring the server

When calling [ Server::new()](https://docs.rs/struct.Server.html#method.new), a mock server with default options is returned from the server
pool. This should suffice for most use cases.

If you’d like to bypass the server pool or configure the server in a different
way, you can use [ Server::new_with_opts](https://docs.rs/struct.Server.html#method.new_with_opts). The following

**options**are available:

- `host`: allows setting the host (defaults to- `127.0.0.1`)
- `port`: allows setting the port (defaults to a randomly assigned free port)
- `assert_on_drop`: automatically call- `Mock::assert()`- `false`)

```
let opts = mockito::ServerOpts { assert_on_drop: true, ..Default::default() };
let server = mockito::Server::new_with_opts(opts);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#matchers)Matchers

Mockito can match your request by method, path, query, headers or body.

Various matchers are provided by the [ Matcher](https://docs.rs/enum.Matcher.html) type: exact (string, binary, JSON), partial (regular expressions,
JSON), any or missing. The following guide will walk you through the most common matchers. Check the

[documentation for all the rest.](https://docs.rs/enum.Matcher.html)

`Matcher`[§](https://docs.rs#matching-by-path-and-query)Matching by path and query

By default, the request path and query is compared by its exact value:

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
// Matches only calls to GET /hello
s.mock("GET", "/hello").create();
// Matches only calls to GET /hello?world=1
s.mock("GET", "/hello?world=1").create();
```
You can also match the path partially, by using a regular expression:

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

```
let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
// Will match calls to GET /hello/1 and GET /hello/2
s.mock("GET",
    mockito::Matcher::Regex(r"^/hello/(1|2)$".to_string())
  ).create();
```
Or you can catch all requests, by using the [ Matcher::Any](https://docs.rs/enum.Matcher.html#variant.Any) variant:

[§](https://docs.rs#example-2)Example

```
let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
// Will match any GET request
s.mock("GET", mockito::Matcher::Any).create();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#matching-by-query)Matching by query

You can match the query part by using the [ Mock::match_query](https://docs.rs/struct.Mock.html#method.match_query) function together with the various matchers,
most notably

[:](https://docs.rs/enum.Matcher.html#variant.UrlEncoded)

`Matcher::UrlEncoded`[§](https://docs.rs#example-3)Example

```
let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
// This will match requests containing the URL-encoded
// query parameter `greeting=good%20day`
s.mock("GET", "/test")
  .match_query(mockito::Matcher::UrlEncoded("greeting".into(), "good day".into()))
  .create();
// This will match requests containing the URL-encoded
// query parameters `hello=world` and `greeting=good%20day`
s.mock("GET", "/test")
  .match_query(mockito::Matcher::AllOf(vec![
    mockito::Matcher::UrlEncoded("hello".into(), "world".into()),
    mockito::Matcher::UrlEncoded("greeting".into(), "good day".into())
  ]))
  .create();
// You can achieve similar results with the regex matcher
s.mock("GET", "/test")
  .match_query(mockito::Matcher::Regex("hello=world".into()))
  .create();
```
Note that the key/value arguments for [ Matcher::UrlEncoded](https://docs.rs/enum.Matcher.html#variant.UrlEncoded) should be left in plain (unencoded) format.

You can also specify the query as part of the path argument in a [ mock](https://docs.rs/struct.Server.html#method.mock) call, in which case an exact
match will be performed:

[§](https://docs.rs#example-4)Example

```
let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
// This will perform a full match against the query part
s.mock("GET", "/test?hello=world").create();
```
If you’d like to ignore the query entirely, use the [ Matcher::Any](https://docs.rs/enum.Matcher.html#variant.Any) variant:

[§](https://docs.rs#example-5)Example

```
let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
// This will match requests to GET /test with any query
s.mock("GET", "/test").match_query(mockito::Matcher::Any).create();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#matching-by-header)Matching by header

By default, headers are compared by their exact value. The header name letter case is ignored though.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-6)Example

```
let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
s.mock("GET", "/hello")
  .match_header("content-type", "application/json")
  .with_body(r#"{"hello": "world"}"#)
  .create();
s.mock("GET", "/hello")
  .match_header("content-type", "text/plain")
  .with_body("world")
  .create();
// JSON requests to GET /hello will respond with JSON, while plain requests
// will respond with text.
```
You can also match a header value with a *regular expressions*, by using the [ Matcher::Regex](https://docs.rs/enum.Matcher.html#variant.Regex) matcher:

[§](https://docs.rs#example-7)Example

```
let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
s.mock("GET", "/hello")
  .match_header("content-type", mockito::Matcher::Regex(r".*json.*".to_string()))
  .with_body(r#"{"hello": "world"}"#)
  .create();
```
Or you can match a header *only by its field name*, by setting the [ Mock::match_header](https://docs.rs/struct.Mock.html#method.match_header) value to

[.](https://docs.rs/enum.Matcher.html#variant.Any)

`Matcher::Any`[§](https://docs.rs#example-8)Example

```
let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
s.mock("GET", "/hello")
 .match_header("content-type", mockito::Matcher::Any)
 .with_body("something")
 .create();
// Requests containing any content-type header value will be mocked.
// Requests not containing this header will return `501 Not Implemented`.
```
You can mock requests that should be *missing a particular header field*, by setting the [ Mock::match_header](https://docs.rs/struct.Mock.html#method.match_header)
value to

[.](https://docs.rs/enum.Matcher.html#variant.Missing)

`Matcher::Missing`[§](https://docs.rs#example-9)Example

```
let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
s.mock("GET", "/hello")
  .match_header("authorization", mockito::Matcher::Missing)
  .with_body("no authorization header")
  .create();
// Requests without the authorization header will be matched.
// Requests containing the authorization header will return `501 Mock Not Found`.
```
[§](https://docs.rs#matching-by-body)Matching by body

You can match a request by its body by using the [ Mock::match_body](https://docs.rs/struct.Mock.html#method.match_body) method.
By default, the request body is ignored, similar to passing the

[argument to the](https://docs.rs/enum.Matcher.html#variant.Any)

`Matcher::Any`[method.](https://docs.rs/struct.Mock.html#method.match_body)

`Mock::match_body`You can match a body by an exact value:

[§](https://docs.rs#example-10)Example

```
let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
// Will match requests to POST / whenever the request body is "hello"
s.mock("POST", "/").match_body("hello").create();
```
Or you can match the body by using a regular expression:

[§](https://docs.rs#example-11)Example

```
let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
// Will match requests to POST / whenever the request body *contains* the word "hello" (e.g. "hello world")
s.mock("POST", "/").match_body(
    mockito::Matcher::Regex("hello".to_string())
  ).create();
```
Or you can match the body using a JSON object:

[§](https://docs.rs#example-12)Example

```
#[macro_use]
extern crate serde_json;
let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
// Will match requests to POST / whenever the request body matches the json object
s.mock("POST", "/").match_body(mockito::Matcher::Json(json!({"hello": "world"}))).create();
```
If `serde_json::json!` is not exposed, you can use [ Matcher::JsonString](https://docs.rs/enum.Matcher.html#variant.JsonString) the same way,
but by passing a

`String` to the matcher:```
let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
// Will match requests to POST / whenever the request body matches the json object
s.mock("POST", "/")
    .match_body(
       mockito::Matcher::JsonString(r#"{"hello": "world"}"#.to_string())
    )
    .create();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-anyof-matcher)The `AnyOf` matcher

The [ Matcher::AnyOf](https://docs.rs/enum.Matcher.html#variant.AnyOf) construct takes a vector of matchers as arguments and will be enabled
if at least one of the provided matchers matches the request.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-13)Example

```
let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
// Will match requests to POST / whenever the request body is either `hello=world` or `{"hello":"world"}`
s.mock("POST", "/")
    .match_body(
        mockito::Matcher::AnyOf(vec![
            mockito::Matcher::Exact("hello=world".to_string()),
            mockito::Matcher::JsonString(r#"{"hello": "world"}"#.to_string()),
        ])
     )
    .create();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-allof-matcher)The `AllOf` matcher

The [ Matcher::AllOf](https://docs.rs/enum.Matcher.html#variant.AllOf) construct takes a vector of matchers as arguments and will be enabled
if all the provided matchers match the request.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-14)Example

```
let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
// Will match requests to POST / whenever the request body contains both `hello` and `world`
s.mock("POST", "/")
    .match_body(
        mockito::Matcher::AllOf(vec![
            mockito::Matcher::Regex("hello".to_string()),
            mockito::Matcher::Regex("world".to_string()),
        ])
     )
    .create();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#custom-matchers)Custom matchers

If you need a more custom matcher, you can use the [ Mock::match_request](https://docs.rs/struct.Mock.html#method.match_request) function, which
takes a closure and exposes the

[object as an argument. The closure should return a boolean value.](https://docs.rs/struct.Request.html)

`Request`[§](https://docs.rs#example-15)Example

```
use mockito::Matcher;
let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
// This will match requests that have the x-test header set
// and contain the word "hello" inside the body
s.mock("GET", "/")
    .match_request(|request| {
        request.has_header("x-test") &&
            request.utf8_lossy_body().unwrap().contains("hello")
    })
    .create();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#asserts)Asserts

You can use the [ Mock::assert](https://docs.rs/struct.Mock.html#method.assert) method to

**assert that a mock was called**. In other words,

`Mock#assert` can validate that your code performed the expected HTTP request.By default, the method expects only **one** request to your mock.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-16)Example

```
use std::net::TcpStream;
use std::io::{Read, Write};
let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
let mock = s.mock("GET", "/hello").create();
{
    // Place a request
    let mut stream = TcpStream::connect(s.host_with_port()).unwrap();
    stream.write_all("GET /hello HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n".as_bytes()).unwrap();
    let mut response = String::new();
    stream.read_to_string(&mut response).unwrap();
    stream.flush().unwrap();
}
mock.assert();
```
When several mocks can match a request, Mockito applies the first one that still expects requests.
You can use this behaviour to provide **different responses for subsequent requests to the same endpoint**.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-17)Example

```
use std::net::TcpStream;
use std::io::{Read, Write};
let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
let english_hello_mock = s.mock("GET", "/hello").with_body("good bye").create();
let french_hello_mock = s.mock("GET", "/hello").with_body("au revoir").create();
{
    // Place a request to GET /hello
    let mut stream = TcpStream::connect(s.host_with_port()).unwrap();
    stream.write_all("GET /hello HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n".as_bytes()).unwrap();
    let mut response = String::new();
    stream.read_to_string(&mut response).unwrap();
    stream.flush().unwrap();
}
english_hello_mock.assert();
{
    // Place another request to GET /hello
    let mut stream = TcpStream::connect(s.host_with_port()).unwrap();
    stream.write_all("GET /hello HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n".as_bytes()).unwrap();
    let mut response = String::new();
    stream.read_to_string(&mut response).unwrap();
    stream.flush().unwrap();
}
french_hello_mock.assert();
```
If you’re expecting more than 1 request, you can use the [ Mock::expect](https://docs.rs/struct.Mock.html#method.expect) method to specify the exact amount of requests:

[§](https://docs.rs#example-18)Example

```
use std::net::TcpStream;
use std::io::{Read, Write};
let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
let mock = s.mock("GET", "/hello").expect(3).create();
for _ in 0..3 {
    // Place a request
    let mut stream = TcpStream::connect(s.host_with_port()).unwrap();
    stream.write_all("GET /hello HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n".as_bytes()).unwrap();
    let mut response = String::new();
    stream.read_to_string(&mut response).unwrap();
    stream.flush().unwrap();
}
mock.assert();
```
You can also work with ranges, by using the [ Mock::expect_at_least](https://docs.rs/struct.Mock.html#method.expect_at_least) and

[methods:](https://docs.rs/struct.Mock.html#method.expect_at_most)

`Mock::expect_at_most`[§](https://docs.rs#example-19)Example

```
use std::net::TcpStream;
use std::io::{Read, Write};
let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
let mock = s.mock("GET", "/hello").expect_at_least(2).expect_at_most(4).create();
for _ in 0..3 {
    // Place a request
    let mut stream = TcpStream::connect(s.host_with_port()).unwrap();
    stream.write_all("GET /hello HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n".as_bytes()).unwrap();
    let mut response = String::new();
    stream.read_to_string(&mut response).unwrap();
    stream.flush().unwrap();
}
mock.assert();
```
The errors produced by the [ Mock::assert](https://docs.rs/struct.Mock.html#method.assert) method contain information about the tested mock, but also about the

**last unmatched request**, which can be very useful to track down an error in your implementation or a missing or incomplete mock. A colored diff is also displayed:

Color output is enabled by default, but can be toggled with the `color` feature flag.

Here’s an example of how a [ Mock::assert](https://docs.rs/struct.Mock.html#method.assert) error looks like:

```
> Expected 1 request(s) to:
POST /users?number=one
bob
...but received 0
> The last unmatched request was:
POST /users?number=two
content-length: 5
alice
> Difference:
# A colored diff
```
You can also use the [ Mock::matched](https://docs.rs/struct.Mock.html#method.matched) method to return a boolean for whether the mock was called the
correct number of times without panicking

[§](https://docs.rs#example-20)Example

```
use std::net::TcpStream;
use std::io::{Read, Write};
let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
let mock = s.mock("GET", "/").create();
{
    let mut stream = TcpStream::connect(s.host_with_port()).unwrap();
    stream.write_all("GET / HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n".as_bytes()).unwrap();
    let mut response = String::new();
    stream.read_to_string(&mut response).unwrap();
    stream.flush().unwrap();
}
assert!(mock.matched());
{
    let mut stream = TcpStream::connect(s.host_with_port()).unwrap();
    stream.write_all("GET / HTTP/1.1\r\n\r\n".as_bytes()).unwrap();
    let mut response = String::new();
    stream.read_to_string(&mut response).unwrap();
    stream.flush().unwrap();
}
assert!(!mock.matched());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#non-matching-calls)Non-matching calls

Any calls to the Mockito server that are not matched will return *501 Not Implemented*.

Note that **mocks are matched in the order they are defined**.

[§](https://docs.rs#cleaning-up)Cleaning up

As mentioned earlier, mocks are cleaned up whenever the server goes out of scope. If you
need to remove them earlier, you can call [ Server::reset](https://docs.rs/struct.Server.html#method.reset) to remove all mocks registered
so far:

```
let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
s.mock("GET", "/1").create();
s.mock("GET", "/2").create();
s.mock("GET", "/3").create();
s.reset();
// Nothing is mocked at this point
```
…or you can call [ Mock::remove](https://docs.rs/struct.Mock.html#method.remove) to remove a single mock:

```
let mut s = mockito::Server::new();
let m1 = s.mock("GET", "/1").create();
let m2 = s.mock("GET", "/2").create();
m1.remove();
// Only m2 is available at this point
```
[§](https://docs.rs#debug)Debug

Mockito uses the `env_logger` crate under the hood to provide useful debugging information.

If you’d like to activate the debug output, introduce the [env_logger](https://crates.rs/crates/env_logger) crate
to your project and initialize it before each test that needs debugging:

```
#[test]
fn example_test() {
    let _ = env_logger::try_init();
    // ...
}
```
Run your tests with:

`RUST_LOG=mockito=debug cargo test`## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- Stores a HTTP request

- [Server](https://docs.rs/struct.ServerOpts.html)- Opts

# assert-json-diff 2.0.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/assert-json-diff/^2.0

# assert-json-diff

This crate includes macros for comparing two serializable values by diffing their JSON
representations. It is designed to give much more helpful error messages than the standard
[ assert_eq!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/macro.assert_eq.html). It basically does a diff of the two objects and tells you the exact
differences. This is useful when asserting that two large JSON objects are the same.

It uses the [serde](https://crates.io/crates/serde) and [serde_json](https://crates.io/crates/serde_json) to perform the serialization.

### Partial matching

If you want to assert that one JSON value is "included" in another use
[ assert_json_include](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_json_include.html):

```
use assert_json_include;
use json;
let a = json!;
let b = json!;
assert_json_include!
```
This will panic with the error message:

```
json atoms at path ".data.users[0].country.name" are not equal:
    expected:
        "Sweden"
    actual:
        "Denmark"
json atoms at path ".data.users[1].id" are not equal:
    expected:
        2
    actual:
        24
```
[ assert_json_include](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_json_include.html) allows extra data in

`actual` but not in `expected`. That is so you can verify just a part
of the JSON without having to specify the whole thing. For example this test passes:```
use assert_json_include;
use json;
assert_json_include!
```
However `expected` cannot contain additional data so this test fails:

```
use assert_json_include;
use json;
assert_json_include!
```
That will print

```
json atom at path ".a.b" is missing from actual
```
### Exact matching

If you want to ensure two JSON values are *exactly* the same, use [ assert_json_eq](https://docs.rs/macro.assert_json_eq.html).

```
use assert_json_eq;
use json;
assert_json_eq!
```
This will panic with the error message:

```
json atom at path ".a.b" is missing from lhs
```
### Further customization

You can use [`assert_json_matches`] to further customize the comparison.

# bytes 1.12.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/bytes/^1

# Bytes

A utility library for working with bytes.

## Usage

To use `bytes`, first add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "1"
```
Next, add this to your crate:

```
use ;
```
## no_std support

To use `bytes` with no_std environment, disable the (enabled by default) `std` feature.

```
[]
 = {  = "1",  = false }
```
To use `bytes` with no_std environment without atomic CAS, such as thumbv6m, you also need to enable
the `extra-platforms` feature. See the [documentation for the  portable-atomic
crate](https://docs.rs/portable-atomic) for more information.

The MSRV when `extra-platforms` feature is enabled depends on the MSRV of `portable-atomic`.

## Serde support

Serde support is optional and disabled by default. To enable use the feature `serde`.

```
[]
 = {  = "1",  = ["serde"] }
```
The MSRV when `serde` feature is enabled depends on the MSRV of `serde`.

## Building documentation

When building the `bytes` documentation the `docsrs` option should be used, otherwise
feature gates will not be shown. This requires a nightly toolchain:

```
RUSTDOCFLAGS="--cfg docsrs" cargo +nightly doc
```

# hyper 1.10.1 - Docs.rs

A protective and efficient HTTP library for all.

- HTTP/1 and HTTP/2
- Asynchronous design
- Leading in performance
- Tested and **correct**
- Extensive production use
- Client and Server APIs

**Get started** by looking over the [guides](https://hyper.rs/guides/1/).

## "Low-level"

hyper is a relatively low-level library, meant to be a building block for libraries and applications.

If you are looking for a convenient HTTP client, then you may wish to consider
[reqwest](https://github.com/seanmonstar/reqwest).

If you are not sure what HTTP server to choose, then you may want to consider
[axum](https://github.com/tokio-rs/axum) or
[warp](https://github.com/seanmonstar/warp), the latter taking a more functional
approach. Both are built on top of this library.

# log 0.4.33 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/log/^0.4

# log

A Rust library providing a lightweight logging *facade*.

A logging facade provides a single logging API that abstracts over the actual logging implementation. Libraries can use the logging API provided by this crate, and the consumer of those libraries can choose the logging implementation that is most suitable for its use case.

## Minimum supported `rustc`

See the `rust-version` field in `Cargo.toml` for the current minimum Rust toolchain version.

This version is explicitly tested in CI and may be bumped in any release as needed. Maintaining compatibility with older compilers is a priority though, so the bar for bumping the minimum supported version is set very high. Any changes to the supported minimum version will be called out in the release notes.

## Usage

### In libraries

Libraries should link only to the `log` crate, and use the provided macros to
log whatever information will be useful to downstream consumers:

```
[]
 = "0.4"
```
```
use ;
```
### In executables

In order to produce log output, executables have to use a logger implementation compatible with the facade. There are many available implementations to choose from, here are some options:

- Simple minimal loggers:
- Complex configurable frameworks:
- Adaptors for other facilities:
- For WebAssembly binaries:
- For dynamic libraries:
- You may need to construct [an FFI-safe wrapper over](https://github.com/rust-lang/log/issues/421)to initialize in your libraries.`log`

- You may need to construct
- Utilities:

Executables should choose a logger implementation and initialize it early in the runtime of the program. Logger implementations will typically include a function to do this. Any log messages generated before the logger is initialized will be ignored.

The executable itself may use the `log` crate to log as well.

## Structured logging

If you enable the `kv` feature, you can associate structured data with your log records:

```
use ;
```
